title: POC scoping: Harbor Financial - latency SLOs & benchmark plan
summary: Discovery / POC scoping focused on defining latency & throughput SLOs for Harbor Financial's generative assistant workload. Discussed TTFT vs TPOT, target p95/p99 numbers, workload sizing (concurrency/qps), measurement harness, and secure deployment constraints (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Agreed next steps: share benchmark harness, security docs, schedule infra deep-dive, and provide pilot quote.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
next_steps: Maya to send SOC2 whitepaper and security FAQ by 2026-11-22
Ravi to share benchmark harness repo + sample scripts by 2026-11-24
Claire to provide canonical prompt set and 2 weeks of anonymized traffic by 2026-11-24
Schedule 2-hour technical deep dive with Harbor infra team week of 2026-11-29
action_items: Maya - send security docs and SOC2 report - due 2026-11-22
Ravi - publish benchmark harness (mock traffic + loader) to shared folder - due 2026-11-24
Claire - share sample prompt set and success criteria doc - due 2026-11-24

transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um we wanted to cover the POC scoping, specifically latency SLOs — TTFT vs TPOT, sizing, benchmarks. I'm Maya from Redwood.
[00:08] Claire: Hi Maya, Claire here. Thanks, we have Jordan and Miguel on as well. We're trying to define clear success criteria before procurement.
[00:13] Miguel: Yeah hi, sorry I'm late, pinged from another call. TL;DR: security and latency are top blockers for exec sign off.
[00:20] Maya: totally, that's what we'll focus on. Ravi our solutions engineer will dive into measurement plan and benchmarks. Ravi?
[00:26] Ravi: hey all, quick agenda: define TTFT (time to first token) and TPOT (time per token), pick p95/p99 targets, estimate workload qps/concurrency, outline benchmark harness and how we'll measure under realistic traffic (KV cache hit rates, prefix caching), and discuss deployment options given Harbor's VPC/KMS constraints.
[00:41] Jordan: For context our main product is an internal assistant that serves trade reconciliation helpers, so average request length is 120 tokens output, prompts vary 60-200 tokens. Peak concurrency seen last quarter was ~120 concurrent active users with long polling for streaming responses. We need to plan for 250 concurrent sessions for headroom.
[00:58] Ravi: good detail. Quick clarif — is the assistant synchronous API (user waits for first token) or do you stream?
[01:04] Claire: it's streaming, user needs first token quickly — perceived latency is what the traders complain about.
[01:09] Ravi: ok so TTFT matters a lot for UX. Two common SLOs: TTFT p95 and p99, and then TPOT for steady-state throughput per token which matters for cost and tail latency.
[01:19] Miguel: can you give ballpark numbers other customers use? We need something exec-friendly.
[01:22] Ravi: sure, ballpark: for low-latency consumer apps TTFT p95 ~50-150ms depending on model & infra; TPOT p95 usually 10-40ms per token on optimized GPU tiling/quant profiles. For financial workloads with stricter SLAs you often see TTFT p95 target 100-200ms and p99 <500ms as a starting point. TPOT p95 15-30ms. Those ranges depend on model size, batching, and whether you use dedicated capacity.
[01:47] Claire: hmm 100ms p95 sounds tight for our models (we run a 30B variant). Our throughput requirement is more important at peak concurrency — we need responses under 3s for typical 120-token output.
[01:58] Ravi: makes sense. Let's translate: for 120-token output, if TTFT p95 = 200ms and TPOT p95 = 25ms, expected p95 total latency = TTFT + (tokens * TPOT) = 0.2 + (120 * 0.025) = 3.2s which is close to 3s target. You can tune model variant or quantization (int8/4) and dedicated GPUs to improve TPOT.
[02:22] Jordan: can you explain tradeoff dedicated vs hosted? We have compliance needs (VPC peering and KMS).
[02:27] Maya: Hosted API gives fastest onboarding, but dedicated gives predictable throughput and single-tenant guarantees; Private (VPC or on-prem) gives full network isolation and customer-managed KMS for data residency — all options can meet latency but cost and setup time differ.
[02:40] Miguel: timeframe wise executive wants a 3-month pilot with SLA-ish targets.
[02:45] Maya: ok good. For pilot we'll propose a dedicated pilot: reserved capacity for peak concurrency, run benchmarks to validate TTFT/TPOT, and a measurement plan with p95/p99 observed over 1-2 week runs.
[02:57] Ravi: measurement plan outline: 1) replicate production traffic profile (arrival patterns, prompt length distribution, cache hot rates), 2) run closed-loop load tests with a gradation to peak concurrency (50%, 75%, 100%, 150%), 3) collect TTFT/TPOT per request with timestamps and tags for cache-hit vs miss, 4) compute p50/p95/p99 and tail cost per million tokens. We'll provide harness that uses your prompt set.
[03:25] Claire: what about KV cache? Our app uses a cache for prefixes; on cache hit TTFT is lower. We expect ~40% prefix hit rate.
[03:33] Ravi: good to capture that — measurement will report cache-hit vs cache-miss buckets. Also important: warm vs cold KV cache for session resumption. We'll simulate session patterns to approximate warm cache.
[03:44] Jordan: any known gotchas in measurement? e.g. network noise, egress, TLS handshake?
[03:49] Ravi: yes network egress, TLS, and your VPC peering can add 10-50ms depending on topology. We'll instrument synthetic tests from your VPC to Redwood endpoints to isolate network vs infer runtime. Also watch for tail amplification due to GC on the host or kernel preemption.
[04:05] Miguel: security: we need KMS for model prompts at rest and SOC2. Are those standard?
[04:11] Maya: yes we support KMS integrations and can run Private control plane if needed, and we have SOC2 docs — I'll send the whitepaper.
[04:18] Claire: back to SLOs — let's propose concrete numbers for the pilot: TTFT p95 <= 200ms, TTFT p99 <= 600ms, TPOT p95 <= 30ms, total request p95 <= 3s for 120 tokens. Are we comfortable?
[04:30] Ravi: that's a realistic starting SLO set for a 30B-ish model on dedicated A10G / H100 equiv with appropriate quantization. If you need stricter TTFT (<=100ms) you'd likely need smaller model or colocated edge infra.
[04:45] Jordan: cost question — what's typical token cost for this profile?
[04:48] Maya: depends a lot, sample numbers: hosted might be X cents per 1k tokens; dedicated lowers per-token compute by ~30-60% due to packing and reserved capacity. We'll provide a cost estimate in the pilot quote.
[04:59] Ravi: also we will run two baseline configs during the benchmark: 1) hosted-curated model (fastest path), 2) dedicated with quantized model and optimized kernel. We'll report TTFT/TPOT curves vs qps.
[05:12] Claire: measurement details: how do you define TTFT exactly? Is it from request timestamp to first token byte on wire?
[05:17] Ravi: good call — we'll define TTFT as time from request receive at Redwood ingress (or at your VPC egress point if we measure network) to first token emitted by the model runtime — we'll measure both edge-to-edge and runtime-only. TPOT is average inter-token time measured at runtime. All measured with p50/p95/p99.
[05:34] Miguel: what about sampling frequency and stats windows — we need to avoid noisy p99 from tiny samples.
[05:40] Ravi: we'll use ≥10k request samples per bucket where feasible and show confidence intervals; for small sample sizes we'll annotate uncertainty. For p99 we recommend at least overnight runs to capture diurnal tails.
[05:52] Claire: log retention and audit: we need per-request logs for the POC but anonymized. Can Redwood redact?
[05:58] Maya: yes we have redaction controls and can do token-level masking, and for Private you can retain logs on your side. We'll send the data handling doc.
[06:06] Jordan: ok, timeline for benchmarks and pilot?
[06:09] Maya: proposed: this week share security docs and harness; week of Nov 29 do infra deep dive and get VPC tested; first week of Dec run baseline benchmarks; week of Dec 14 run pilot validation and present results to exec. So ~6 weeks to baseline + validation.
[06:24] Claire: that timeline works internally if we can get the harness and VPC creds quickly.
[06:28] Ravi: one more technical note: TPOT can be improved by batching but batching trades latency. For streaming UX you typically use micro-batching or continuous batching with limits on max latency per token. We'll include parameterized experiments in the harness to show latency vs throughput curves.
[06:44] Miguel: about measurement harness — do you provide end-to-end scripts for us to run inside our network?
[06:48] Ravi: yes we'll provide a dockerized load generator that can run inside your VPC, plus a Redwood-side collector. It will tag each request with run-id, prompt id, cache-hit boolean, and we'll provide dashboards.
[06:58] Claire: demo expectations — can you show a before/after with quantization?
[07:01] Ravi: yes we'll include quantized vs FP16 vs smaller model baselines in the benchmark matrix.
[07:06] Maya: ok let's capture explicit success criteria for the pilot so procurement can sign off. Claire, Miguel — you suggested exec needs explicit numbers?
[07:13] Claire: yes: 1) TTFT p95 <= 200ms; 2) TPOT p95 <= 30ms; 3) end-to-end p95 for 120-token response <= 3s; 4) operation under 250 concurrent sessions with no more than 5% error rate; 5) meeting data handling & SOC2 controls validated.
[07:31] Maya: good. We'll include those as acceptance criteria in the pilot proposal.
[07:35] Jordan: what about rollback/fallback? If dedicated capacity is saturated at peak, we need a fallback to a larger-model hosted path?
[07:41] Ravi: Redwood supports smart routing policies — you can route to a compatible variant or a lower-cost fallback with degraded latency. We'll include a fallback policy in the pilot config.
[07:51] Miguel: can you run initial load tests on a Friday night? smaller network traffic window?
[07:55] Ravi: yes we'll coordinate with Jordan for an off-peak run during the baseline week.
[08:00] Claire: any other open questions?
[08:02] Miguel: just procurement — we need an estimated cost for 3-month pilot with dedicated capacity.
[08:07] Maya: we'll put together a pilot quote with reserved capacity and expected token costs, and include optional dedicated support.
[08:12] Claire: ok sounds good.
[08:14] Maya: recap of next steps — I'll send security docs and SOC2 whitepaper; Ravi will share the benchmark harness and initial scripts; Claire will share prompt set; Jordan will arrange VPC peering details. We'll schedule a 2-hour technical deep dive week of Nov 29. Anything else?
[08:30] Jordan: nope that's it. Thanks everyone.
[08:33] Maya: thanks all, end call.

Notes: occasional transcription errors — "KV cash" heard in some auto transcript lines, proper nouns like model names sometimes mis-recognized. Timestamp cadence is approximate; full logs will be in the shared benchmark harness results.
